Prepared for GP, Occupational Health, and Clinical Review
CLINICAL CONTEXT & STYLE NOTE
This document is written in the style commonly utilised by GPs, Occupational Health physicians, and consultant
psychiatrists. It concentrates on objective clinical information and functional impact, rather than legal issues.

work over many years.
My condition has been recognised by both my employer and the Group Income Protection insurer throughout my
period of absence.

despite attempts at vocational rehabilitation.

13.After I became aware that Mr Khaira had left CACI in or around 2024, I felt, for the first 
time, able to seek assistance in relation to my situation. In or around December 2025, as my 
financial and administrative position continued to deteriorate, I approached Unite Legal 
Services for advice. I did so because my disability substantially affects my ability to initiate 
and navigate complex legal processes without external support, particularly where matters 
are prolonged, adversarial, or administratively complex.
14.Unite advised me that my Equality Act claims were unlikely to succeed on the basis that I 
was not actively attending the workplace and that any duty on CACI to make reasonable 
adjustments would only arise if and when I returned to work. I relied on that advice and did 
not pursue proceedings at that stage, understanding it to mean that there was no lawful 
mechanism available to me to challenge my continuing exclusion.

provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.
From 2001 to 2021, the Claimant received monthly payslips by post from CACI Limited. However,

tax status.

the period in question.

Appendix D – Payslip Request & Evidence of 
Breach
Mr. Arshad Shafi v. CACI Limited
1. Background
Under Section 8 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, employers are under a statutory duty to 
provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.
From 2001 to 2021, the Claimant received monthly payslips by post from CACI Limited. However, 
in 2021, these payslips abruptly ceased without explanation. The Claimant was left without payslips
or P60s for a period of four years (2021–2025), creating uncertainty over his pay, deductions, and 
tax status.
In August 2025, the Claimant formally requested copies of payslips and P60s from the Respondent. 
The Respondent subsequently admitted the omission and supplied retrospective documentation for 
the period in question.

Mr. Arshad Shafi v. CACI Limited
1. Background
Under Section 8 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, employers are under a statutory duty to 
provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.
From 2001 to 2021, the Claimant received monthly payslips by post from CACI Limited. However, 
in 2021, these payslips abruptly ceased without explanation. The Claimant was left without payslips
or P60s for a period of four years (2021–2025), creating uncertainty over his pay, deductions, and 
tax status.
In August 2025, the Claimant formally requested copies of payslips and P60s from the Respondent. 
The Respondent subsequently admitted the omission and supplied retrospective documentation for 
the period in question.

This appendix records the continuity of corporate leadership within CACI Limited relevant to the 
Claimant’s employment and subsequent dispute.

approximately 26 years’ service) and Mr Jeet Khaira (former Managing Director, Information & 
Management Systems Division, departed 2024) both held senior executive roles during and after the
period 2000 – 2005 that forms the basis of the Claimant’s case.

of the events underlying this claim and continued access to relevant HR, occupational-health and 
insurer (Unum) records.

provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.

Appendix L5 – Leadership Continuity (Weir 
and Khaira)
Claimant: Mr Arshad Shafi
Respondent: CACI Limited
Bundle Section: Part 10 – Appendices
Date prepared: October 2025
Summary
This appendix records the continuity of corporate leadership within CACI Limited relevant to the 
Claimant’s employment and subsequent dispute.
It confirms that Ms Tracy Weir (President & Chief Executive since November 2024, with 
approximately 26 years’ service) and Mr Jeet Khaira (former Managing Director, Information & 
Management Systems Division, departed 2024) both held senior executive roles during and after the
period 2000 – 2005 that forms the basis of the Claimant’s case.
Their overlapping tenures demonstrate that CACI Ltd retains long-standing institutional knowledge 
of the events underlying this claim and continued access to relevant HR, occupational-health and 
insurer (Unum) records.

1. Background
Under Section 8 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, employers are under a statutory duty to 
provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.
From 2001 to 2021, the Claimant received monthly payslips by post from CACI Limited. However, 
in 2021, these payslips abruptly ceased without explanation. The Claimant was left without payslips
or P60s for a period of four years (2021–2025), creating uncertainty over his pay, deductions, and 
tax status.
In August 2025, the Claimant formally requested copies of payslips and P60s from the Respondent. 
The Respondent subsequently admitted the omission and supplied retrospective documentation for 
the period in question.

provide employees with an itemised pay statement for each pay period.

tax status.

element_records.legal_significance: Evidence about the claimant's condition, duration and functional effects is relevant to the factual basis of the disability requirement.
element_records.provisional_analysis: The frozen evidential record provides partial factual support relevant to the factual basis of disability at the relevant time, but material limitations remain. The current record may describe the condition and functional effects without finally determining the statutory definition. Medical or sickness evidence alone does not amount to a final finding that the statutory disability definition is met.

Prepared for GP, Occupational Health, and Clinical Review
CLINICAL CONTEXT & STYLE NOTE
This document is written in the style commonly utilised by GPs, Occupational Health physicians, and consultant
psychiatrists. It concentrates on objective clinical information and functional impact, rather than legal issues. 
2. MEDICAL BACKGROUND
Long-Term Mental Health Condition
I have experienced a long-term psychiatric illness since 2001, which has had a significant impact on my ability to
work over many years.
My condition has been recognised by both my employer and the Group Income Protection insurer throughout my
period of absence.
Following a relapse during 2005, I remained employed by CACI Ltd but was unable to return successfully to work
despite attempts at vocational rehabilitation.

element_records.legal_significance: Evidence linking absence, behaviour, need, incapacity or another circumstance to disability is relevant to identifying the alleged 'something arising'.
element_records.provisional_analysis: The frozen evidential record provides partial factual support relevant to the factual link between disability and the identified consequence or circumstance, but material limitations remain. The current record may support a provisional factual connection between disability and the circumstance relied upon. Temporal association or claimant assertion alone does not finally establish that the circumstance arose in consequence of disability for statutory purposes.

source_assertions.text:
Source assertion: Occupational Health concludes that a return to work is medically appropriate, I believe the following measures
should be considered:
Phased Return
A gradual increase in working hours and responsibilities would allow my response to work to be monitored and
reviewed.
Home Working
Given the significant impact of prolonged commuting on my mental health, home working or predominantly home-
based hybrid working may substantially reduce unnecessary stress and fatigue.
Gradual Increase in Duties
Initially limiting workload and complexity, with planned progression as confidence and resilience improve, may
improve the prospects of a successful rehabilitation.
Regular Reviews
Regular review meetings with Occupational Health and my manager would enable progress to be monitored and
adjustments made where necessary.
Workplace Adjustments
Examples that may merit consideration include:
home working or hybrid working;
flexible start and finish times;
a quieter working environment;

source_assertions.text:
Source assertion: able to challenge my treatment.
13.After I became aware that Mr Khaira had left CACI in or around 2024, I felt, for the first 
time, able to seek assistance in relation to my situation. In or around December 2025, as my 
financial and administrative position continued to deteriorate, I approached Unite Legal 
Services for advice. I did so because my disability substantially affects my ability to initiate 
and navigate complex legal processes without external support, particularly where matters 
are prolonged, adversarial, or administratively complex.
14.Unite advised me that my Equality Act claims were unlikely to succeed on the basis that I 
was not actively attending the workplace and that any duty on CACI to make reasonable 
adjustments would only arise if and when I returned to work. I relied on that advice and did 
not pursue proceedings at that stage, understanding it to mean that there was no lawful 
mechanism available to me to challenge my continuing exclusion.
